diet.note: Stomach contents are preserved in the larger of the two specimens described in 1998. Mammal jaws once reported inside a 'Sinosauropteryx' (NGMC/GMV 2124) are now attributed to a small tyrannosauroid (Qiu et al. 2025), so they are not used here.

timeRange.note: S. prima comes from the Jianshangou bed of the Yixian Formation near Sihetun (PBDB). The range is the U-Pb bracket for the whole Yixian Formation in the Jin-Yang basin (Zhong et al. 2021); the Jianshangou unit lies inside it. PBDB's stage-based range is wider (125.77 to 119.57 Ma).

lengthM.note: Museum figure for the genus. The 1.2 m holotype of the second species, S. lingyuanensis, is described as the largest known Sinosauropteryx specimen (Qiu et al. 2025), so S. prima specimens are smaller.

massKg.note: Single estimate from limb-bone robustness scaling; standard error 0.135 log10(kg).

summary.en: Sinosauropteryx was a small meat-eater, about a metre long, that lived around 125 million years ago in what is now north-eastern China. Its body was covered in simple, hair-like filaments, and in 1996 it became the first non-bird dinosaur found with evidence of feather-like structures. It had a remarkably long tail, and stomach contents show it hunted small animals. Fossil pigments suggest a dark back, pale belly, striped tail and a dark mask across its eyes.

text.en: Pigment traces on S. prima fossils show countershading (dark above, light below), a banded tail and a 'bandit mask' around the eyes, a pattern that suggests it lived in fairly open habitats.
The famous reddish-brown colour reconstruction from 2010 was based on specimen IVPP V 14202. In 2025 that specimen became the holotype of a separate genus, Huadanosaurus.

uncertain.note: Kept in Compsognathidae, the traditional placement. Qiu et al. (2025) group the Jehol compsognathid-like theropods in a separate clade, Sinosauropterygidae, because Compsognathus falls outside it in one of their analyses; PBDB also lists Sinosauropterygidae. Hendrickx (2025) notes a 2024 study suggesting compsognathids may be an artificial group of juveniles of other theropods.
No peer-reviewed length for S. prima specimens was verified; only a museum figure for the genus is given.
